# Laurance Lee 林灼世
SFUSD gave me my start. I’m running to help every child get the same chance.
As the son of an undocumented Chinese immigrant, I struggled early in school. San Francisco public-school teachers helped me find my footing and opened opportunities that changed my life. Today, I volunteer weekly helping kindergartners learn to read and work across SFUSD to turn good intentions into results.
You have three votes for School Board. I’m asking for one.
Endorsed by State Senator Scott Wiener, the Chinese American Democratic Club, IUEC Local 8 and UFCW Local 648.
Supported by SFUSD educators and parents across San Francisco.

My Story
# Coming Back
"Are you coming back tomorrow?"
It was the first question a kindergarten teacher asked me, after my first morning as a literacy volunteer.
"Of course," I said.
She smiled. "Many volunteers don't."
I kept thinking about that conversation over the following months. I still do. It's part of why I'm running for the San Francisco Board of Education.
I grew up in SFUSD — Argonne Elementary, Presidio Middle School, Lowell High School — the son of an undocumented Chinese immigrant. Our public schools became a second home. I struggled with a childhood speech impediment, and with challenges I'd later understand as part of my neurodivergence. My teachers saw strengths in me I hadn't found in myself yet.
In eighth grade, one of those teachers, Ms. Rueda, believed I could compete in MATHCOUNTS, the nation's premier middle school math competition. I placed first in San Francisco and among the top four students in California, earning a spot on the state's four-student team. Ms. Rueda took time off work and drove us to Sacramento herself. We finished second in the nation.
Four years later, my chemistry teacher, Mr. Becker, spent countless hours outside of class mentoring me. In 1988, I was one of four students selected to represent the United States at the International Chemistry Olympiad in Helsinki, Finland, where I earned a Silver Medal.
I wasn't a child with extraordinary advantages. I was a kid from an immigrant family who had two teachers willing to invest their own time in me. That changed the course of my life — Harvard, then a career trying to cure cancer as a biotech researcher, work recognized with a Merck research award, and later a shift into construction, working on residential real estate projects across the Bay Area and other states as a licensed general contractor.
I never really left our schools behind. I volunteered with students through college, supported classroom projects through DonorsChoose, helped raise funds for another elementary school, served on the San Francisco Civil Grand Jury, and became Vice Chair of SFUSD's Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee, helping oversee more than $1 billion in school construction investments.
Earlier this year, I realized there was still one perspective I was missing. I understood budgets, bond oversight, and curriculum. But if I wanted to help lead SFUSD, I wanted to understand what those decisions looked like from inside a classroom.
Through the SF Education Fund, I began volunteering each week with a small literacy group in a kindergarten classroom.
One student had entered school months after the year began and was still learning her letters. We practiced together every week. On the last day of school, she handed me a handwritten thank-you note with a picture she'd drawn. A few months earlier, I'd been helping her write the letter Y.
Another student was frequently absent because she and her sister spent hours commuting across the city each morning. I couldn't change that. But I tried to make sure she knew I was genuinely happy every time she walked in. By the end of the year, she always wanted to show me her newest stickers before we got to work.
I found myself watching the teacher as closely as the students. She adjusted lessons constantly. She expected a great deal from her students because she believed they were capable of more. When I offered to help buy classroom supplies, she told me many families were working multiple jobs just to get by — the school didn't even have a PTA. Watching her work each week gave me a deeper appreciation for what great teachers ask of themselves.
The more time I spent in that classroom, the more I thought about my own teachers — Ms. Rueda, Mr. Becker, and so many others who saw something in me before I could see it myself. Sitting beside those kindergartners, I understood their work in a way I never could have as a student.
Those months changed how I think about the role of a school board. My professional background taught me how organizations improve through evidence, planning, and accountability. That classroom reminded me that every budget, every policy, and every decision eventually reaches a child. Schools aren't all at the same point in their journey — some need stronger literacy support, some need help improving attendance, others are ready to expand opportunities for advanced learners. Good governance means understanding those differences and helping every school keep moving forward.
Every budget, every policy, and every decision eventually reaches a child.
That's why I keep coming back. I came back to the schools that shaped me. I came back because I still had more to learn. And I'm running because I want every family in San Francisco to believe our public schools are moving in the right direction. — Laurance Lee

## A Life in San Francisco Public Schools
1970s
Born and raised in San Francisco, the son of an undocumented Chinese immigrant.
1980s
Attends Argonne Elementary, Presidio Middle School, and Lowell High School; places 1st in San Francisco and top 4 in California at MATHCOUNTS (1984); represents the United States at the International Chemistry Olympiad in Helsinki, Finland, earning a Silver Medal (1988).
1990s
Graduates Harvard; works as a biotech researcher trying to cure cancer, recognized with a Merck research award.
2010s
Licensed general contractor, working on residential real estate projects across the Bay Area and other states.
2020s
Serves on the San Francisco Civil Grand Jury; becomes Vice Chair of SFUSD's Citizens' Bond Oversight Committee, overseeing $1B+ in school construction; volunteers weekly in a kindergarten classroom through the SF Education Fund; runs for San Francisco Board of Education.

# Chronic Absenteeism
The $60 Million Silent Crisis — and How SF Schools Are Already Fighting Back
Students can’t learn if they’re not in school.
“Nearly one in four SFUSD students is chronically absent. That costs us more than $60 million in lost funding and millions of hours of learning. The good news: some of our own schools are already proving we can turn it around.”
— Laurance Lee
## The Reality in 2026
- SFUSD chronic absenteeism: ~24% (Red on the California Dashboard)
- State average: ~19.5–20%
- Learning hours lost (2024-25): 4.4 million
- State funding lost: over $60 million
- Low-income students ≈ 33% | Students with disabilities ≈ 35%
When students miss 10% or more of the school year, reading and math gains stall, graduation risk rises, and the entire district loses resources that should be in classrooms.
## When Plans Don’t Reach Schools
What is an SPSA? The School Plan for Student Achievement is a school’s public improvement plan: it records student needs, goals, planned actions, staffing and funding. SFUSD says school communities use it to review data and prior actions, while the elected School Site Council helps develop and monitor the plan and budget. That makes the SPSA one of the clearest places for families to compare what a school said it needed with what actually reached students. See SFUSD’s explanation and the School Site Council’s role.
In Rosa Parks Elementary’s 2023–24 SPSA, the school reported that budget changes removed the assistant principal role. When the new principal later went on leave, there was no administrative backup. The same plan says that, with no family liaison and no principal, no one was coordinating outreach to families of chronically absent students.
The school deserves credit for documenting the problem honestly. SFUSD’s responsibility is to make sure a staffing gap does not become a year without support—and to show families whether promised positions and resources actually reached their school.
## Local Proof: Guadalupe Elementary Leading the Way
Guadalupe Elementary (Excelsior/Crocker-Amazon) is a high-needs, majority-Latino school with a large English Learner population.
After the pandemic, chronic absenteeism hit roughly 50%. Through strong principal leadership (Raj Sharma), consistent family outreach, targeted interventions, and activities that build belonging (including a thriving soccer program), the school drove major improvement. Rates fell sharply over two years and have remained better than the post-pandemic crisis peak — even as the district overall ticked upward. Math scores are also rising, and the school has posted impressive early literacy gains through high-impact tutoring.
This is exactly the kind of focused, relationship-driven work we need to scale.
## Willie L. Brown Middle School — A Broader Turnaround Story
Willie Brown shows what strong leadership and a culture of belonging can achieve. Once one of the district’s most challenged schools, it is now fully enrolled with a waitlist. Test scores have risen dramatically (ELA 25% → 51%; math 8% → 33%) and student growth scores are strong. Attendance improved as part of the overall culture shift, though the principal has noted that the most chronically underperforming subgroups still need more targeted support. It stands as powerful proof that high expectations + belonging work in the southeast.
## What California Bright Spots Teach Us
Districts such as Bakersfield (–33 points), Livingston, Cypress, Roseville, and Paradise cut chronic absenteeism sharply with real-time data, relationship-based outreach, home visits, removing barriers, and positive recognition.
## My Plan
- Give high-need schools a trained attendance lead—and backup coverage when a principal or family liaison is absent.
- Use timely, student-level attendance data so teams can act before a pattern becomes chronic.
- Fund family outreach, home visits and practical help with transportation, health and other barriers.
- Scale belonging strategies that are working at schools such as Guadalupe and Willie Brown.
- Report attendance, learning time and funding effects by school and student group every quarter.
## Day One vs. Year One
Day One: Publish the attendance support and vacancy picture by school, identify campuses without a responsible attendance lead, and start simple quarterly reporting.
Year One and beyond: Build stable school-based teams, expand proven family outreach and belonging strategies, and tie funding to measurable attendance improvement.

- SFUSD/SPARK “Be Here!” announcement — 4.4 million learning hours and more than $60 million in funding lost in 2024–25.
- 2025 California School Dashboard: SFUSD and CDE chronic-absence data files.
- Rosa Parks Elementary 2023–24 SPSA and SFUSD’s Rosa Parks data page.
- The Frisc: Guadalupe’s attendance work.
